## How is version control used currently? {style="text-align: center;"}

- File changes are tracked in remote git repositories
- Commits are snapshots of the project files at a given point in time
- Code files are easily stored in git repositories, like storing photos in a photo album
 
:::: {.columns}
 
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](An Introduction to Data Version Control (DVC)_files/images/Git Diagram.png){width=90%}
:::
 
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](An Introduction to Data Version Control (DVC)_files/images/photos into album.png){width=90%}
:::
 
::::

::: {.notes}
We all know what git is? This is the most common method of version control, where changes to files are tracked in a remote git repository in the form of commits (snapshots of the project files at a given point in time). Files are easily stored in git repositories, like storing photos in a photo album.
:::

## What makes version control difficult in data science? {auto-animate="true"}

::: {.notes}

So what makes version control difficult in data science? We not only have code, but also data and models to keep track of. Models will change depending on data and code so this is a lot of changes to keep track of. If you're keeping track of the files manually, you may name them all differently depending on the changes you make (give some examples). These days, data scientists work with huge datasets that are too large to store in a git repository. It would be like trying to shove the yellow pages into a photo album. 

:::

- Open-source tool with a command-line interface and python API.
- Allows git-like versioning of data, models and model pipelines.
- Tracks the metadata of the data and models, while the actual data and models are stored in a remote storage (e.g. S3, Google Drive, Azure Blob Storage, locally).

:::

## How does our git know about the data?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

![](An Introduction to Data Version Control (DVC)_files/images/dvc file.png)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

![](An Introduction to Data Version Control (DVC)_files/images/dvc file contents.png){width=70%}
:::

::::

::: {.smaller}

- DVC uses a .dvc file to store the metadata of the data. This is tracked in git.
- The .dvc file contains the path to the data, the hash of the data, and the hashing algorithm that was used to generate the hash.

:::

::: {.notes}

If we're not storing the data in the git repository, how does our git know about the data? It tracks the metadata instead by using a .dvc file. The .dvc file contains the path to the data, the hash of the data, and the hash of the code that was used to generate the data. If you were to look in your dvc repository, you would see the data file at the time of this commit under that hash. This is how dvc know's which version of the data to get according to the state of the code at the time of this commit.
:::

## DVC pipelines

- With dvc, you can keep track of data and models at different stages of the machine learning lifecycle.
- By setting dependencies, you have essentially performed a `dvc add` action.
- The data that is set as a dependency is now tracked in the dvc pipeline.

```bash
dvc stage add -n preprocessing \
  -d src/preprocessing.py -d data/raw/lego_sets.csv \
  -o data/processed/preprocessed_lego_sets.csv \
  poetry run python src/preprocessing.py
```
::: {.notes}
We can use dvc stage add to set up a dvc pipeline. We name the stage, specify the dependencies, outputs, and command to run the stage.

:::

## dvc.yaml

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

![](An Introduction to Data Version Control (DVC)_files/images/dvc yaml file.png){width=90%}

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

- The dvc.yaml file contains the pipeline definition.
- Here, you can track each stage of the pipeline, including inputs, dependencies, outputs, and commands that run the stages.
- No need to run individual stages manually.

:::

::::

::: {.notes}
This is the file that contains the information of the pipeline. It has the names of the stages, the dependancies, the outputs, and the command to run the stage.
:::

## dvc.lock file

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

![](An Introduction to Data Version Control (DVC)_files/Images/dvc lock file.png)

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

- The dvc.lock file contains the metadata of the pipeline.
- This is tracked in git along with the dvc.yaml file.
- This is what dvc uses to know which version of the data and code to use at each stage of the pipeline.

:::

::: {.notes}
This is the file that contains the metadata of the pipeline. It is tracked in git along with the dvc.yaml file. It's not overly readable but it's how dvc knows which version of the data and code to use at each stage of the pipeline.
:::

::::

## Updating stages and reproducing the pipeline {auto-animate="true"}


::: {.notes}

Running dvc repro will run the pipeline. If you are running it for the first time, all stages will be run. Subsequently, if one of the stages in the pipeline changes, dvc will only run that stage and the stages that depend on it. This because each run of the pipeline is cached, and dvc can see which steps have been run already. This dramatically speeds up the development cycle of your model.
:::

## A change in hash means a bust in cache {auto-animate="true"}

## A change in hash means a bust in cache {auto-animate="true"}

- DVC has a run cache, where each of the runs of the pipeline is stored.

## A change in hash means a bust in cache {auto-animate="true"}

- DVC has a run cache, where each of the runs of the pipeline is stored.
- DVC looks at this cache and compares the hash of the dependencies to those in the dvc.lock file.

## A change in hash means a bust in cache {auto-animate="true"}

- DVC has a run cache, where each of the runs of the pipeline is stored.
- DVC looks at this cache and compares the hash of the dependencies to those in the dvc.lock file.
- If the hash has changed, dvc will run the stage again.

## A change in hash means a bust in cache {auto-animate="true"}

- DVC has a run cache, where each of the runs of the pipeline is stored.
- DVC looks at this cache and compares the hash of the dependencies to those in the dvc.lock file.
- If the hash has changed, dvc will run the stage again.
- This is true if the code that the stage depends on has changed as well.

::: {.notes}

Running dvc repro will run the pipeline. If you are running it for the first time, all stages will be run. Subsequently, if one of the stages in the pipeline changes, dvc will only run that stage and the stages that depend on it. This because each run of the pipeline is cached, and dvc can see which steps have been run already. This dramatically speeds up the development cycle of your model.
:::

## Parameters

- Parameters can be used to change the behaviour of a stage in the pipeline.
- Parameters are specified in params.yaml file.
- Parameters can be added to the pipeline using the `-p` flag.

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width=50%}

![](An Introduction to Data Version Control (DVC)_files/images/params.png){width=90%}

:::

:::{.column width=50%}

![](An Introduction to Data Version Control (DVC)_files/images/dvc yaml params.png){width=90%}

:::

::::

::: {.notes}
You can use parameters to change the behaviour of a stage in the pipeline. Parameters are specified in params.yaml file - you will have to create this yourself. Parameters can be added to the pipeline using the `-p` flag, or you can manually specify the parameters in the dvc.yaml file. In this example, we have parameters for the random state, number of estimators, and max depth of the random forest model.

:::

## Experiment tracking with DVC

- You can specify metrics to track in the dvc.yaml file.
- You can then use the dvc python API to log metrics.

![](An Introduction to Data Version Control (DVC)_files/images/metrics yaml.png){width=90%}

```python
from dvclive import Live

with Live("data/evaluation") as live:
    for metric, value in metrics.items():
        live.log_metric(metric, value)
```

![](An Introduction to Data Version Control (DVC)_files/images/vs code.png){width=90%}

## Plots

- Plots are specified in the dvc.yaml file.

```python
with Live(str(plot_dir), resume=True) as live:
        live.log_image("feature_importance.png", fig)
```
![](An Introduction to Data Version Control (DVC)_files/images/plots.png){width=90%}

## Queueing up experiments in DVC

- You can queue up experiments in DVC and have them run successively.
- This can be helpful for hyperparameter tuning.

```bash
dvc exp run --queue -S 'train.n_estimators=range(50, 100, 10)' -S 'train.max_depth=range(5, 10, 1)'
```
![](An Introduction to Data Version Control (DVC)_files/images/dvc queue.png){width=90%}

- You can run `dvc queue start` to kick off the experiments.

## This is all well and good locally. But what about in the cloud? {align="center"}

![](An Introduction to Data Version Control (DVC)_files/images/Technology Cloud GIF by puraenvidia.gif){width=90%}


## DVC produces generic files
 - DVC does not produce file types that are specific to a framework. They are generic file types such as yaml, csv, pkl, etc.
 - This means that your dvc code can be wrapped and used with other ML frameworks, including:
    - Amazon Sagemaker
    - Databricks
    - Huggingface
    - Evidently
